newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb victims lose bid to witness trial.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb victims lose bid to witness trial.

text.p: A federal appeals court on Tuesday said victims of the Oklahoma City bombing who plan to testify at the upcoming trial may not be permitted to sit in the courtroom to hear other testimony.

In a 3-0 decision the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals in Denver dismissed the victims' appeal on grounds they did not have "legal standing" to seek review of the trial judge's ruling that barred them from the courtroom.
The decision is a blow for family members and other victims of the April 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that claimed 168 lives.

"I am really angry. We had expected to win this," said Marsha Kight, whose daughter Frankie Merrell died in the blast. "People are just getting fed up with the judicial system. Everyone is getting very frustrated," she said.
The appeals court noted that the Victims' Rights Act, upon which the families relied for their appeal, specifically bars victims from suing over provisions of the act.
Ordinarily, witnesses who testify at federal trials may not sit in the courtroom and hear other testimony, lest they be influenced by it.
But in this case victims, who must already travel to Denver for the trial, hoped they could change the court's mind.
Victims would be testifying at the penalty phase of the case if either defendant is convicted. Victims who do not plan to testify will be able to sit in the courtroom.

Kight said she had planned to testify at the penalty portion, but cannot do so unless the decision is overturned. "I am going to be in that courtroom every day and I have every right to be," she said. Kight and other family members have faithfully attended the pre-trial hearings in Denver.
She said she expected the victims would appeal the decision to a higher court.
The court also dismissed a companion appeal from prosecutors on behalf of the victims, saying the government had no right to appeal the trial judge's decision.
Timothy McVeigh and former army buddy Terry Nichols have been charged in the bombing and face the death penalty.
They will be tried separately, with McVeigh going first on March 31. Nichols will be tried at a later undetermined date.
